name: How do attached ADU plans handle natural light and privacy on tight lots?

mainEntity.name: If the addition is close to neighboring homes, how can the design provide light without exposing the unit to privacy issues?
mainEntity.text: If the addition is close to neighboring homes, how can the design provide light without exposing the unit to privacy issues?

acceptedAnswer.text: Natural light and privacy are often in tension on tight urban lots, especially in Los Angeles-area neighborhoods where homes sit close together. Attached ADUs usually solve this with a mix of higher window placement, clerestory windows, skylights, light wells, and strategically oriented glazing. The goal is to brighten the unit without creating direct sightlines into neighboring yards, bedrooms, or patios. Privacy can also be improved by using frosted glass in bathrooms, solid wall sections in sensitive areas, and small screened outdoor zones rather than large open terraces. A good design team will map both interior daylight and exterior views before settling on the window plan. This question often gets less attention than cost or size, but it strongly affects comfort and resale appeal. The best ADU feels open and bright without making occupants feel exposed. That balance usually requires custom design, not just a stock floor plan.
acceptedAnswer.description: Attached ADU designs on tight lots often use higher windows, clerestory openings, skylights, and carefully placed glass to bring in light while protecting privacy. The layout should avoid direct views into neighboring yards or bedrooms and may need frosted glass or screened outdoor areas.
